title: Incident severity and response
description: Learn about Incident severity and response. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: **Incident severity and response** are the backbone of production operations. How you classify and react to incidents determines whether a minor blip becomes a headline. This lesson teaches you to define severity levels, build response playbooks, and lead teams through high-pressure situations with clarity.
What Is an Incident

An incident is an unplanned interruption or degradation of a service that affects users. Not every alert is an incident, and not every incident requires a page. Define the incident threshold explicitly: a service is in incident when the SLI drops below the SLO target and users are demonstrably impacted. Health check failures that do not affect user traffic are noise, not incidents.

terms.definition: An unplanned interruption or degradation of service that affects real users.
A classification of incident impact that determines response urgency and escalation.
The person responsible for coordinating the response, making decisions, and communicating status.
The engineer who receives the page and begins initial investigation and mitigation.
A dedicated communication channel where responders coordinate in real time.

data.title: Senior Engineer Mindset
data.text: Do not page on every alert. Page only when the incident threshold is crossed: real user impact, sustained degradation, and no automatic recovery. Calibrate your paging policy monthly to prevent alert fatigue.
Incident Severity Levels

Most organizations define four severity levels. Severity one is a complete outage with widespread user impact and revenue loss. Severity two is a major degradation affecting a significant user segment. Severity three is a minor issue affecting a small subset of users with a workaround available. Severity four is an internal issue with no user impact. Map each level to response time expectations and escalation paths.

rows: Complete outage, widespread user impact, revenue loss
Major degradation, significant user segment affected
Minor issue, small user segment, workaround available

data.text: Severity Classification Criteria

Severity should be based on user impact, not infrastructure metrics. A service can be at 50 percent CPU and be SEV-3 if only internal admins are affected. A service can be at 80 percent CPU and be SEV-1 if checkout is failing for 40 percent of users. Use criteria that non-engineers can understand: users affected, revenue impact, data loss, and regulatory risk.

items: Users affected: number of active users impacted
Revenue impact: estimated revenue loss per hour
Data loss: irreversible loss of user data or transaction records
Regulatory risk: potential legal or compliance consequences
Media coverage: likelihood of public attention

data.text: Incident Detection

Incidents are detected through three channels: automated alerts, user reports, and synthetic monitoring. Automated alerts from Prometheus, Datadog, or CloudWatch are the fastest but can produce false positives. User reports through support tickets or social media are slower but highly reliable. Synthetic monitoring from external probes catches issues before users notice. Use all three channels and deduplicate alerts to avoid noise.

items: Automated alerts: configure multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts on SLI metrics
User reports: feed support tickets into the incident management system via webhook
Synthetic monitoring: deploy external probes that test critical user journeys every 60 seconds
Deduplication: aggregate related alerts into a single incident ticket

data.text: The Incident Response Lifecycle

Every incident follows a lifecycle: detect, respond, mitigate, recover, and review. Detection triggers the page. Response is the initial assessment and triage. Mitigation is the action that stops the bleeding. Recovery is restoring full service. Review is the postmortem and action-item tracking. Each phase has a time-box and a clear owner.

items: Detect: alert fires or user reports issue
Respond: on-call acknowledges, assesses severity, declares incident
Mitigate: implement fix or workaround to stop user impact
Recover: verify full service restoration and monitor for regressions
Review: write postmortem, assign action items, update runbooks

data.text: Response Time Expectations

Response time expectations should be written into the on-call runbook. SEV-1 incidents require acknowledgement within 15 minutes. SEV-2 within 30 minutes. SEV-3 within 2 hours. Measure these expectations with real data and publish the metrics monthly. If the team consistently misses SEV-1 response times, reduce the paging blast radius or add more on-call engineers.

data.title: Response Time SLO
data.text: Track acknowledgement time as a percentage of incidents acknowledged within the target window. Aim for 95 percent compliance for SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents.
On-Call Runbooks

Every alert should link to a runbook that tells the on-call engineer exactly what to do. The runbook should include the alert description, the likely causes, the step-by-step mitigation procedure, the rollback command, the escalation contact, and the incident channel link. Runbooks should be reviewed after every incident and updated whenever the system changes.
Incident Triage Process

Triage is the art of rapidly understanding an incident and deciding the response strategy. The on-call engineer should acknowledge the alert within the response window, open an incident ticket, assess severity, page additional responders if needed, and start initial investigation. A good triage process prevents SEV-1 incidents from being handled as SEV-3 because of misclassification.

items: Acknowledge the alert within the response time window
Open an incident ticket with timestamp, alert name, and affected service
Assess severity based on user impact, not infrastructure metrics
Page additional responders if the service is unfamiliar or the blast radius is large
Start initial investigation while waiting for responders

data.text: Communication During Incidents

Communication is the hardest part of incident response. The incident commander should post status updates every 15 minutes for SEV-1 and every 30 minutes for SEV-2. Updates should state what is known, what is being done, and the expected next update. Do not speculate about root cause until it is confirmed. Use a dedicated incident channel and pin the status update for visibility.

items: Post status updates every 15 minutes for SEV-1
Post status updates every 30 minutes for SEV-2
Use a dedicated incident channel and pin updates
Communicate to customers through status page and support team

data.text: Incident Command Roles

Clear roles prevent chaos during an incident. The **incident commander** owns the process, coordinates responders, and makes go or no-go decisions. The **technical lead** owns the investigation and mitigation strategy. The **communications lead** owns internal and external status updates. The **scribe** documents the timeline and decisions. Assign roles at the start of every SEV-1 and SEV-2 incident.

cards.title: Incident Commander
cards.description: Coordinates the response, assigns tasks, makes decisions, and communicates to leadership. Does not perform technical investigation.

cards.title: Technical Lead
cards.description: Leads the technical investigation, decides on mitigation strategy, executes fixes. Does not manage communications.

cards.title: Communications Lead
cards.description: Posts status updates to the incident channel, updates the status page, and communicates with customer success.

cards.title: Scribe
cards.description: Documents the incident timeline, decisions, and actions in real time for the postmortem.

data.text: Incident Triage Decision Tree

A decision tree helps on-call engineers classify incidents quickly. Start with the user impact: are users affected? If yes, is the service completely down or degraded? If degraded, is there a workaround? If there is no workaround, classify as SEV-1. If there is a workaround, classify as SEV-2. If no users are affected, classify as SEV-3 or SEV-4.

data.title: Incident Triage Decision Tree
data.content: Use this decision tree to classify incidents quickly. Adapt it to your service portfolio and user base.

data.text: Mitigation Strategies

Mitigation is the action that stops or reduces user impact. Common strategies include rollback, feature flag kill, traffic shifting, rate limiting, circuit breaking, and scaling. Choose the strategy that minimizes time to recovery. A rollback takes minutes but loses the new feature. A fix takes hours but preserves the feature. The incident commander should weigh the trade-offs and make a clear decision.

items: Rollback: revert to the last known good deployment
Feature flag kill: disable the feature without rolling back
Traffic shifting: route traffic away from the degraded region or service
Rate limiting: reduce traffic to prevent cascading failure
Circuit breaking: stop calling a failing dependency
Scaling: add capacity to absorb traffic spikes

data.text: Escalation Policies

Escalation policies define who to page and when. A typical policy escalates from the primary on-call to the secondary on-call after 10 minutes, to the team lead after 20 minutes, and to the engineering manager after 30 minutes for SEV-1 incidents. Escalation should be automatic through PagerDuty or Opsgenie, not manual. Document the policy in the runbook and test it quarterly.

data.title: Escalation Drift
data.text: Escalation policies drift when team members leave or change roles. Audit the on-call rotation and escalation policy quarterly. Ensure every level has a primary and a backup.
Incident Timelines

The scribe should maintain a real-time timeline of the incident. Each entry includes a timestamp, the actor, the action taken, and the outcome. The timeline becomes the foundation of the postmortem. Use a shared document or the incident management tool to capture it. Do not rely on memory after the incident ends.

data.title: Incident Timeline Format
data.content: Each timeline entry follows a simple format: timestamp, actor, action, outcome. This makes the postmortem factual and easy to write.
data.code:
14:02 UTC | Alice (on-call) | Acknowledged alert, opened incident ticket
14:03 UTC | Alice | Checked dashboards, identified payment gateway timeouts
14:05 UTC | Alice | Paged Bob (payment service owner)
14:08 UTC | Bob | Joined incident channel, confirmed gateway issue
14:12 UTC | Alice | Rolled back last deployment, error rate dropped
14:15 UTC | Alice | Declared mitigated, updated status page
14:20 UTC | Bob | Created postmortem draft
14:30 UTC | Alice | Closed incident ticket

data.text: Mitigation Decision Framework

When choosing a mitigation strategy, the incident commander should evaluate four factors: time to implement, reversibility, user impact, and technical risk. A feature flag kill is fast and reversible but might expose users to inconsistent behavior. A rollback is fast and safe but loses the new feature. A hotfix is slower but preserves the feature. The framework helps the team make consistent decisions under pressure.

items: Time to implement: how many minutes or hours to deploy?
Reversibility: can the fix be undone quickly?
User impact: does the fix itself cause disruption?
Technical risk: does the fix introduce new failure modes?

data.text: Rollback as a Mitigation Strategy

Rollback is the most common mitigation strategy and should be the default for any deployment-induced incident. Every service should have a documented rollback procedure that the on-call engineer can execute without asking for permission. Automate rollback where possible with canary analysis and automated promotion gates. A one-click rollback reduces mean time to recover from hours to minutes.

data.title: Automated Rollback
data.text: Configure canary analysis to automatically roll back when the error rate exceeds the SLO. The on-call engineer still investigates, but the system stops the bleeding.
Feature Flag Kill

Feature flags let you decouple deployment from launch. If a new feature causes errors, kill the flag instead of rolling back the entire deployment. This preserves other changes in the same deploy and reduces the blast radius. Every new feature should be behind a flag by default. Define a maximum flag kill time in the runbook so the on-call engineer does not hesitate.

items: Launch new features behind feature flags
Document the flag kill command in the runbook
Test the flag kill procedure in staging before production
Kill the flag first, investigate second

data.text: Traffic Shifting

Traffic shifting moves load away from a degraded region or service. Use DNS failover, load balancer weight changes, or service mesh traffic splitting. The shift should be automatic if possible but manual override should always be available. Document the traffic shifting commands in the runbook and test them in staging.

items: DNS failover: change DNS TTL to low values during normal operation
Load balancer weight: shift 100 percent to healthy region
Service mesh: use traffic mirroring and shifting rules
Manual override: keep console access for emergency use

data.text: Rate Limiting and Circuit Breaking

Rate limiting protects a service from traffic spikes. Circuit breaking stops a service from calling a failing dependency. Both are essential mitigation strategies. Configure rate limits based on the service capacity and the SLO. A service that handles 1000 RPS should have a rate limit of 1200 RPS to absorb spikes. A circuit breaker should trip after 50 percent error rate over 30 seconds.

data.title: Circuit Breaker Configuration
data.content: Configure circuit breakers with error thresholds and recovery windows. This prevents cascading failures when a downstream service degrades.

data.text: Incident Communication Channels

Every incident should have a dedicated communication channel. Use Slack or Teams for real-time coordination, a shared incident document for the timeline, and a status page for external communication. The channel name should follow a convention such as #incident-sev1-payment-2024-01-15 so it is searchable. Pin the status update and the runbook link to the channel.
Status Page Management

The status page is the single source of truth for customers during an incident. Update it within 15 minutes of declaring an incident. Use plain language: do not say we are experiencing elevated error rates. Say some users are unable to complete checkout. Provide estimated time to resolution when known and update the page every 30 minutes.

data.title: Status Page Best Practice
data.text: Always include an estimated recovery time or a statement that the team is actively investigating. Silence on the status page is interpreted as indifference.
Customer Communication During Incidents

Customer success should be looped in for SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents. They can proactively notify affected customers, answer support tickets, and manage executive escalations. Provide customer success with a one-sentence summary they can share: what is broken, who is affected, and what is being done. This prevents them from guessing or over-promising.

items: Loop in customer success for SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents
Provide a one-sentence summary for support team distribution
Give customer success the expected resolution timeline
Brief the customer success lead every 30 minutes

data.text: Incident Severity Drift

Severity classifications drift when the criteria are not explicit or when teams have different interpretations. Audit incident classifications quarterly. If the same alert is classified as SEV-2 by one on-call engineer and SEV-3 by another, the criteria need tightening. Use a shared severity rubric and include it in the on-call runbook.

items: Publish a shared severity rubric in the runbook
Use real incident examples in on-call training

data.text: Post-Incident Recovery

Recovery is not just restoring service. It is verifying that the service is fully operational, monitoring for regressions, and communicating the resolution. After mitigation, the on-call engineer should run a smoke test of critical user journeys, monitor the SLI for 30 minutes, update the status page to resolved, and send a final notification. Only then should the incident be closed.

items: Run smoke tests of critical user journeys
Update status page to resolved with root cause summary
Close the incident ticket only after all checks pass

data.text: Incident Metrics to Track

Track incident metrics to improve response performance over time. Mean time to acknowledge, mean time to mitigate, mean time to recover, and percentage of incidents acknowledged within the SLA. Publish these metrics in a monthly incident review. Compare them against industry benchmarks and set improvement goals.
Incident Review Meetings

Hold a weekly or bi-weekly incident review meeting for the engineering organization. Review all incidents from the period, discuss response performance, and identify systemic improvements. The meeting should be blameless and focused on process improvement. Invite representatives from engineering, product, and customer success.

data.title: Incident Review Format
data.text: Each incident gets 5 minutes: timeline, response performance, root cause, action items. Focus on patterns, not individual incidents.
Incident Simulation Training

Train the on-call team with incident simulations. Fire a simulated alert, observe the response, and debrief. Rotate the incident commander role so everyone practices leadership. Use game-day platforms such as Gameday or Chaos Monkey to automate simulation scenarios. Run at least one simulation per quarter per team.

items: Run a tabletop exercise every quarter
Run a production-like simulation every six months
Rotate incident commander among on-call engineers

data.text: Incident Severity and Remote Teams

Remote teams face unique challenges in incident response. Time zones mean the incident commander might be asleep when the incident starts. Overlapping on-call shifts and async communication tools mitigate this. Use a follow-the-sun on-call model with at least two hours of overlap between shifts. Document the incident commander handoff process so the incoming commander is fully briefed.

items: Async handoff document with full incident context
Use video calls for complex incidents requiring real-time collaboration
Record war room sessions for asynchronous review

data.text: Incident Severity and Vendor SLA

Vendor outages affect your incident severity. If a cloud provider has a regional outage and your service is down, classify the incident based on your user impact, not the vendor's root cause. The incident commander should document the vendor impact in the timeline and track it for vendor SLA claims. Maintain a vendor incident contact list so you can escalate during their outage.

data.title: Vendor Claims
data.text: Document vendor-caused incidents with timestamps and impact evidence. Submit SLA credit claims within the vendor's required timeframe, typically 30 days.
Incident Severity and Legal Considerations

Some incidents have legal implications. Data breaches, privacy violations, and regulatory non-compliance require immediate legal involvement. The incident response plan should include a legal escalation path. For GDPR-related incidents, notify the data protection authority within 72 hours. For PCI-DSS incidents, follow the breach notification procedure in the compliance manual.

items: Define legal escalation triggers in the incident response plan
Notify legal counsel for data breaches and privacy incidents
Document all actions for regulatory compliance

data.text: Incident Severity and Public Relations

Public relations should be involved for incidents with media potential. A SEV-1 outage that affects a popular consumer app will likely be covered by tech press. Prepare a holding statement in advance that the communications team can adapt. Do not let engineers speak to the press without PR review. The statement should be factual, empathetic, and focused on remediation.

items: Prepare a holding statement template for SEV-1 incidents
Brief the communications lead within 30 minutes of declaration
Route all media inquiries through PR
Post the public statement on the status page and company blog

data.text: Incident Severity and Insurance

Cyber insurance policies often require evidence of incident response maturity. Maintain documentation of your severity classification, response times, runbooks, and postmortems. This documentation supports insurance claims and demonstrates due diligence. Some policies require notification within 24 hours of a breach. Ensure the incident response plan includes insurance notification steps.

data.title: Insurance Documentation
data.text: Maintain incident response documentation, severity classifications, and postmortems as evidence for cyber insurance claims. Notify the insurer within the policy-required timeframe.
Incident Severity and Business Continuity

Incident severity should align with the business continuity plan. A SEV-1 incident that affects the primary revenue stream should trigger the business continuity team. A SEV-3 incident affecting internal tools does not. Define the escalation path to business continuity in the incident response plan and test it annually.

items: SEV-1 affecting revenue: trigger business continuity team
SEV-2 affecting significant users: notify business continuity lead
SEV-3 and SEV-4: normal incident response, no continuity activation

data.text: Incident Severity and Crisis Management

For incidents with existential risk to the company, such as a data breach affecting all users or a complete platform outage during a product launch, activate the crisis management team. This team includes the CEO, CTO, legal counsel, and PR lead. The incident commander remains the technical lead but reports to the crisis management team for strategic decisions.

data.title: Crisis Management Activation Criteria
data.content: Define explicit criteria for crisis management activation. This removes ambiguity during high-stress incidents.

data.text: Incident Severity and Remote Work

Remote work changes incident response dynamics. Engineers might not have reliable internet or access to corporate VPNs. Define a remote incident response plan that includes VPN-less access to critical tools, mobile-friendly runbooks, and backup communication channels such as SMS or phone calls. Test the remote access path quarterly.

items: VPN-less access to critical tools via cloud consoles
Backup communication via SMS and phone

data.text: Incident Severity and Diversity

Diverse incident response teams make better decisions. Ensure the on-call rotation includes engineers from different backgrounds, time zones, and seniority levels. Diverse perspectives catch edge cases that a homogeneous team might miss. Measure on-call rotation diversity quarterly and adjust if the team is not representative.

data.title: Diverse Teams
data.text: Diverse on-call rotations improve incident response quality. Include junior engineers, remote workers, and underrepresented groups in the rotation.
Incident Severity and Documentation

Every incident should be documented in a consistent format. The incident ticket should include the alert name, the time of detection, the time of mitigation, the severity classification, the root cause, the action items, and the error budget impact. Use a template so the scribe does not have to think about format during the incident.

data.title: Incident Ticket Template
data.content: Use a consistent template for all incident tickets. This ensures the postmortem is easy to write.
data.code:
INCIDENT_TICKET_TEMPLATE = {
    "alert_name": "payment-gateway-timeout",
    "detected_at": "2024-01-15T14:02:00Z",
    "mitigated_at": "2024-01-15T14:12:00Z",
    "severity": "SEV-1",
    "user_impact": "40% of checkout attempts failing",
    "root_cause": "Payment gateway certificate expired",
    "mitigation": "Rolled back to previous deployment",
    "error_budget_consumed": "15 percent",
    "action_items": ["Add certificate expiry monitoring", "Automate certificate rotation"]
}

data.text: Incident Severity and Continuous Learning

Every incident is a learning opportunity. After the postmortem, the team should conduct a lessons-learned session. What did we do well? What could we improve? How do we prevent this from happening again? Document the lessons in a shared knowledge base and reference them during onboarding. Over time, the knowledge base becomes a training resource for new on-call engineers.

items: Conduct a blameless lessons-learned session after every SEV-1
Document lessons in a shared knowledge base
Update runbooks based on lessons learned

data.text: Incident Severity and Psychological Safety

Blameless postmortems require psychological safety. If engineers fear punishment for declaring incidents or admitting mistakes, they will under-report and under-response. Leadership must explicitly state that incident response is a team activity and that mistakes are learning opportunities. Reward engineers who declare incidents early and participate fully in postmortems.
The severity of an incident is determined by its impact, not by who caused it.
Incident Severity and Career Development

Incident response is a core skill for senior engineers. Being an effective incident commander, a calm technical lead under pressure, and a clear communicator during crises are all markers of seniority. Include incident response performance in engineering performance reviews. Recognize engineers who consistently improve response times and reduce budget consumption.

items: Include incident response in performance reviews
Recognize engineers who improve response times
Provide incident command training for senior engineers
Use incident scenarios in promotion interviews

data.text: Incident Severity and Knowledge Management

The knowledge gained during incidents should be captured and shared. Write internal blog posts about interesting incidents, present at engineering all-hands, and contribute to the team wiki. Knowledge management turns individual incidents into organizational learning. The best teams have a culture of sharing incident stories so that every engineer benefits from every incident.

data.title: Knowledge Sharing
data.text: Write an internal blog post after every SEV-1 incident. Present it at the next engineering all-hands. Turn individual learning into organizational knowledge.
Incident Severity and Tooling

Good tooling reduces cognitive load during incidents. Use PagerDuty or Opsgenie for paging, Slack for communication, Confluence or Notion for runbooks, and Grafana for dashboards. Automate incident ticket creation from alerts. Integrate the observability platform with the incident management tool so the timeline is populated automatically.
Incident Severity and Cost

Incidents cost money. A SEV-1 outage that lasts two hours on a $1 million monthly revenue stream costs approximately $2,800 in direct revenue loss, plus reputational damage and engineering time. Track incident cost alongside error budget impact. This data is persuasive when requesting reliability investments.

data.title: Incident Cost Calculation
data.content: Calculate the direct and indirect cost of an incident. Use this in budget requests for reliability improvements.
data.code:
monthly_revenue = 1_000_000
hourly_revenue = monthly_revenue / (30 * 24)
outage_hours = 2
engineering_cost = 5 * 200  # 5 engineers * $200/hour
direct_cost = hourly_revenue * outage_hours
indirect_cost = direct_cost * 0.5  # Reputational damage estimate
total_cost = direct_cost + engineering_cost + indirect_cost
print(f"Total incident cost: ${total_cost:,.0f}")
# Total incident cost: $9,167

data.text: Incident Severity and Organizational Learning

The best organizations turn every incident into a learning opportunity. They share incident stories widely, celebrate good responses, and use data to drive improvement. They do not blame individuals or hide incidents. They treat incident response as a team sport and measure team performance, not individual performance.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Incident severity should be based on user impact, not infrastructure metrics.
Define explicit severity levels with response time expectations and escalation paths.
Communication during incidents is as important as technical mitigation.
Clear roles prevent chaos during high-pressure situations.
Track incident metrics and review them regularly.
Every incident is a learning opportunity for the entire organization.
data.takeaway: Mastering incident severity and response turns chaos into coordinated action and builds organizational resilience.

items.question: How do I classify an incident as SEV-1 versus SEV-2?
items.answer: SEV-1 is a complete outage with no workaround and widespread user impact. SEV-2 is major degradation with a workaround or a significant user segment affected.

items.question: What is the most common mistake during incident response?
items.answer: Poor communication. Engineers dive into investigation without updating stakeholders. Post status updates every 15 minutes for SEV-1.

items.question: Should I roll back or fix forward?
items.answer: Roll back first to stop user impact, then fix forward in a subsequent deploy. Never fix forward during an active incident unless rollback is impossible.

items.question: How often should I update the status page?
items.answer: Every 15 minutes for SEV-1 and every 30 minutes for SEV-2. Even if there is no progress, post an update.

items.question: Who should be the incident commander?
items.answer: The most experienced on-call engineer for the affected service, or the engineering manager if the incident spans multiple teams.
